```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(formex)
o <- fx_ontology()

## Which ontology rows are "geographic". Geography is a cross-cutting domain, not
## a data_type: these rows live under several data types, so they are pulled
## together in the Geography section at the end and a pointer is left behind in
## each home section.
is_geo <- function(df)
  (df$data_type == "categorical" & df$semantic_type   == "geographic") |
  (df$data_type == "identifier"  & df$semantic_type   == "geographic") |
  (df$data_type == "number"      & df$semantic_family == "coordinate") |
  (df$data_type == "structured"  & df$semantic_family == "geometry")  |
  (df$data_type == "text"        & (df$semantic_type  == "place" |
                                    df$semantic_family == "postal"))

## Collapse ontology rows to one row per group (the meaning, the known
## formats/units, and the detector). `extra = TRUE` prepends a data_type column,
## used by the cross-cutting Geography table.
.collapse <- function(df, by, extra = FALSE) {
  parts <- lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(df)), by), function(ix) {
    g  <- df[ix, , drop = FALSE]
    fl <- unique(g$format_label)
    ut <- unique(g$unit_type[!is.na(g$unit_type) & nzchar(g$unit_type)])
    fu <- paste0("`", paste(fl, collapse = "`, `"), "`")
    if (length(ut)) fu <- paste0(fu, "<br><span style='opacity:.7'>unit: ",
                                 paste(ut, collapse = "; "), "</span>")
    row <- data.frame(
      family        = g$semantic_family[1],
      semantic_type = paste0("**", g$semantic_type[1], "**"),
      meaning       = g$short_desc[1],
      `formats / units` = fu,
      detector      = paste0("`", paste(unique(g$match_kind), collapse = " / "), "`"),
      check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    if (extra) cbind(data_type = paste0("**", g$data_type[1], "**"), row,
                     stringsAsFactors = FALSE) else row
  })
  do.call(rbind, parts)
}

## One table per data_type, with geography rows pulled out and an optional
## pointer note added in their place.
ont_section <- function(dt, note = NULL) {
  s   <- o[o$data_type == dt, , drop = FALSE]
  s   <- s[!is_geo(s), , drop = FALSE]
  tab <- .collapse(s, s$semantic_type)
  tab <- tab[order(tab$family), ]
  if (!is.null(note))
    tab <- rbind(tab, data.frame(
      family = "", semantic_type = "<em>* geographic</em>",
      meaning = paste0("<em>", note, "</em>"),
      `formats / units` = "", detector = "",
      check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
  knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
}

## The cross-cutting Geography table: every geographic row, across data types.
geo_table <- function() {
  g   <- o[is_geo(o), , drop = FALSE]
  tab <- .collapse(g, paste(g$data_type, g$semantic_family, g$semantic_type),
                   extra = TRUE)
  ord <- c("number", "identifier", "categorical", "text", "structured")
  tab <- tab[order(match(gsub("[^a-z]", "", tab$data_type), ord),
                   tab$family, tab$semantic_type), ]
  knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
}
```

The **ontology** is the shared catalog at the center of `formex`: a small,
labeled map of every kind of column research data contains. Both halves of the
package read it --- `guess_data_type()` to decide *where a column belongs*, and
`fx_stabilize()` to look up *how to clean it*. This guide walks the map one
**data type** at a time.

## How the map is organized

Every entry sits at four levels of increasing specificity:

```
data_type        how should it be treated?     number · text · temporal · ...
 └ semantic_family   what broad kind?           date · currency · geographic · ...
    └ semantic_type     what exactly?           calendar · usd · us_state · ...
       └ format_style / unit_type   how written / what unit?
```

The top level, **`data_type`**, is the load-bearing one: it decides whether a
column is a quantity you can do math on, a label you must leave untouched, a
point in time, and so on. The sections below are organized by it. Each opens with
what the type *is* and how it differs from the types it is most often confused
with, followed by the families and semantic types inside it.

### The detector column

Not every type can be recognized just by looking at the values, and the ontology
is honest about which can. Each type records *how* it is spotted, in a
`match_kind` --- shown as the **detector** column in every table below:

| detector | spotted by |
|---|---|
| **`genome`** | a flexible date/time reader that tries many formats |
| **`mask`** | a fixed written shape, sometimes with a self-checking digit |
| **`lexicon`** | membership in a known list of allowed values |
| **`mask+lexicon`** | the right shape *and* a match in a known list |
| **`shape`** | the overall look of the numbers (range, decimals, sign) |
| **`none`** | cannot be told from the values alone --- only a name or data dictionary can |

That last row matters for honesty. A membership-number column is just integers; a
notes column is just text. No amount of looking at the values reveals what they
are, so the ontology marks these `none` and the engine does not pretend.

```{r counts}
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(data_type = o$data_type),
                           responseName = "entries"))
```

Those totals count geographic entries under their home data type (coordinates
under `number`, GEOIDs under `identifier`, and so on); the final **Geography**
section gathers them back together in one place.

---

## `number` --- quantities you can do math on

A `number` is a magnitude: something you can meaningfully add, average, or
compare. This is the type to get right first, because it licenses arithmetic.

**Not to be confused with `identifier`.** A ZIP code, a county FIPS, and an
account number are all written with digits, but they are *labels*, not
magnitudes --- averaging them is nonsense and dropping their leading zeros
corrupts them. If digits are a quantity, they are a `number`; if they are a key,
they are an `identifier`. The `currency` family carries a `unit_type`, because
the same written number can mean dollars or euros. Geographic **coordinates** are
numbers too --- a lat/lon pair is a measurement on a datum --- but they are
gathered with the rest of geography in the Geography section at the end.

```{r number}
ont_section("number", note = "geographic coordinates (lat / lon) are numbers — see the Geography section below")
```

## `text` --- strings, from free prose to structured tokens

`text` covers values whose content is characters: names, email addresses, URLs,
colors, and free-form notes. (Place names and postal addresses are geographic
text, gathered in the Geography section at the end.) Some text is highly
structured (an email, a hex color) and gets a scheme-specific recipe; some is
genuinely free (`text.long`) and is simply preserved.

**Not to be confused with `categorical`.** A `text` column's values are open-ended
--- a new row can introduce a name or note never seen before. A `categorical`
column draws from a *fixed, closed* set of levels. "City name typed in freely" is
text; "one of five survey response options" is categorical.

```{r text}
ont_section("text", note = "place names and postal addresses are text — see the Geography section below")
```

## `temporal` --- points and spans in time

`temporal` values live on a timeline: a calendar date, a timestamp, a quarter, a
day-of-week. They are detected by a flexible reader (`genome`) that recognizes
many written forms and normalizes them to ISO. The `period` and `phase` families
cover coarser or cyclic time (a fiscal quarter, a month-of-year), where a
`unit_type` such as the fiscal convention can matter.

**Not to be confused with `number`.** `2019` could be a count or a year; `3.15`
could be a measurement or a fragment of a date. What makes a column `temporal` is
that its values *locate something in time*, which the reader confirms by parsing
them as such.

```{r temporal}
ont_section("temporal")
```

## `categorical` --- a value from a fixed set of levels

A `categorical` column takes one value from a closed vocabulary: a Likert
response, a classification code, a set of tags. The level-to-label mapping lives
in a dictionary alongside the data; the ontology records only the *shape* of the
encoding.

**Not to be confused with `boolean` or `text`.** A `boolean` is the special case
of exactly two levels that mean true/false. Free strings with no fixed set are
`text`. Many categorical types are `none`-detected: a column of codes `1, 2, 3`
cannot be told from a count without its labels.

```{r categorical}
ont_section("categorical", note = "geographic groupings (state, country, city) — see the Geography section below")
```

## `boolean` --- a two-state flag

A `boolean` is a yes/no, true/false, present/absent flag. `formex` recognizes a
wide vocabulary of encodings (`yes/no`, `t/f`, `1/0`, `active/inactive`, a bare
`x` check) and maps them all to `TRUE`/`FALSE`.

**Not to be confused with `categorical`.** A boolean is *exactly* two states that
collapse to logical true/false. Three or more mutually exclusive levels are
categorical. The one thing that cannot be defaulted is the blank policy --- a
blank is *missing* in a survey but *FALSE* in a checkbox --- so the encoding
records it explicitly.

```{r boolean}
ont_section("boolean")
```

## `identifier` --- keys and codes that must be preserved exactly

An `identifier` labels something: an EIN, an ISBN, a DOI, a record key, a
geographic GEOID (see the Geography section at the end). The defining rule is that
its written form *is* the data ---
leading zeros, delimiters, and check digits all matter --- so it must never be
coerced to a number or silently reformatted.

**Not to be confused with `number`.** This is the most consequential distinction
in the whole ontology, because treating an identifier as a number is how real
data gets corrupted (`06037` → `6037`). Identifiers are detected by `mask` (a
fixed shape, often with a checksum) and sometimes a `lexicon` of valid codes;
`record` and `entity` keys are `none`, knowable only from context.

```{r identifier}
ont_section("identifier", note = "geographic keys (FIPS / GEOID) are identifiers — see the Geography section below")
```

## `structured` --- composite values with internal parts

A `structured` value packs more than one field into a single cell: a JSON object,
a WKT geometry (geographic geometries are gathered in the Geography section at the
end), an array, a key-value blob. It is detected by the syntax of the container
and is typically handled by parsing or splitting into component variables.

**Not to be confused with `categorical` tags.** A `multiselect` tag list is a flat
set of labels; a `structured` value has real internal syntax (brackets, braces,
coordinates) that a parser must honor.

```{r structured}
ont_section("structured", note = "geographic geometries (point, polygon) — see the Geography section below")
```

## `unknown` --- the honest fallback

`unknown` is where a column lands when the values cannot support any type: a
column mixing dates, numbers, and prose (`heterogeneous`), a column of corrupt
values (`malformed`), or one that simply did not resolve (`unclassified`). It is
deliberately part of the ontology, so the engine always has a safe, truthful
place to stop rather than forcing a wrong guess.

```{r unknown}
ont_section("unknown")
```

---

## `geography` --- a cross-cutting domain, not a data type

Geography is the one case that deliberately does **not** get its own `data_type`,
and it is worth saying why. The top level of the ontology classifies *how a value
should be treated, not what domain it is about* --- and a geographic value can
need completely different handling depending on the column it sits in. The *same
place* can be three data types at once: `"Los Angeles County"` the **label**,
`06037` the **key**, and `34.3, -118.2` the **coordinate**.

So geographic entries are distributed across the data types above. Here they are
gathered in one place, with a `data_type` column so the split is explicit:

```{r geography}
geo_table()
```

Why each case lands where it does:

- **`number` --- coordinates.** A latitude/longitude pair is a *measurement* on a
  datum (its `unit_type` is a coordinate reference system such as EPSG:4326). You
  interpolate it, compute distances, reproject it --- all arithmetic --- so it is
  a number.
- **`identifier` --- geographic keys.** A FIPS or GEOID like `06037` is a *key*
  you join on. Its leading zero and fixed width are load-bearing, so it must stay
  text and is hardened (`FIPS-06037`) against a spreadsheet silently turning it
  into `6037`. Taking its average is meaningless.
- **`categorical` --- groupings.** A state or country used to *group* rows
  (`us_state`, `iso_country`) is a factor you analyze *by*: a closed vocabulary,
  matched against a lexicon.
- **`text` --- place names and addresses.** A freely typed city name or a street
  address is open-ended text --- a new row can introduce one never seen before ---
  so it is handled as text, not as a closed category.
- **`structured` --- geometries.** A WKT point or polygon packs coordinates into a
  single cell with real internal syntax that a parser must honor.

So when you meet a geographic column, the useful question is not "is this
geography?" but "which **treatment** does it need?" --- and the answer places it
under the matching data type, with that type's recipe for cleaning and storing it.

---

## Stable identities, so a label means the same thing next year

Every entry carries a stable `semantic_type_id` (like `n0059`) and `variant_id`
(like `n0059-f01`) that are assigned once and never reused. Types are *retired*
rather than deleted, so a label you record today still means the same thing years
from now. `fx_ontology()` reads the whole map; `fx_validate_ontology()` checks it
is internally consistent.

## Where to go next

```
